New episode of my "Vibe Coding till I reach one paying customer" series.
Footage is in C:\Users\edmem\Videos\OBS\Webcam\Video Cuts\Vibe Coding Ep 1 Kodely. Run this mostly autonomously — don't check in with me
at every step, use your judgment based on what's established below, and only
stop for things that are genuinely ambiguous or expensive to undo.

SETUP (read first, don't narrate this back to me):
- tools/video-use/templates/vibe-coding-series/README.md
- tools/video-use/LIQUID_GLASS_STYLE.md
- first-video/edit/scripts/composite_full.py as the reference implementation
  — read the actual functions (build_webcam_primary, build_screen_primary,
  overlay_chain, _hero_transform, main's transition-boundary logic), don't
  just skim the file. Every autonomous decision below has a working
  implementation somewhere in this file; find it and adapt it rather than
  reinventing the technique.
- Reuse first-video/edit/animations/slot_retrowave_bg_loop,
  slot_neon_border_loop, slot_grain_flicker_loop as-is unless this episode's
  content genuinely needs something different.

AUTONOMOUS DECISIONS (make the call yourself, don't ask):

Cut & pacing:
- Take selection, cut placement, pacing — use the established cut-craft
  rules (audio-first, preserve peaks, pad 30-200ms, snap to word boundaries).

Layout per beat:
- Full-webcam-hero vs. screen-recording+PIP for each beat — hero for pure
  talking-head/story sections, PIP for anything referencing what's on
  screen.
- PIP corner (bottom-left/bottom-right): check what's actually on screen at
  each placement, not just alternating corners arbitrarily — reposition
  away from anything the box would cover, with a smooth eased slide (never
  an instant teleport) when the corner changes mid-beat.
- The neon border must be present on the webcam at ALL times it's visible —
  hero mode, PIP mode, and through every PIP corner-to-corner slide — always
  tracking the webcam's exact current box/position, never static or
  disappearing during a transition.

Motion graphics:
- Which moments get a motion graphic — ground each one in a specific
  number/name/callout actually said, not generic decoration. Prefer a few
  well-placed graphics over covering every beat.
- Every motion-graphic card gets the CRT power-on/power-off transition
  (helpers/crt_transition.py) on entrance and exit — except a graphic that's
  a pure continuation across a hard footage cut (still mid-appearance, not a
  true first-appearance or final-disappearance), which should skip that
  edge rather than look like it's glitching/re-powering-on.
- Which graphic-carrying webcam-hero moments need the shrink-aside treatment
  (webcam scales to 60-70% of hero size and moves to whichever side is clear
  of the graphic, rather than cutting to tiny PIP mode). For each one: check
  the graphic's actual rendered content bounding box across its FULL
  duration, not just its opening frame — a placement that's clear at frame 1
  can still collide with the graphic later in its own animation. This
  exact mistake shipped once already this episode (a card and the aside
  webcam box overlapped because only the opening frame was checked) — verify
  with real frame extraction across the graphic's entire active window
  before considering a placement done, and require a genuine deliberate gap,
  not just "technically not touching by a couple pixels."
- Background scrim: a black overlay on the retrowave background PLATE ONLY
  (never the webcam/border/graphic content) — default 25% opacity, composited
  before the border/webcam are drawn on top. Skip the grain/flicker texture
  unless it's specifically wanted for this episode.

Zoom:
- Screen-recording beats only. Genuine focal points only — never decoration
  on broad layout commentary. Cap 2.0x. Verify targets against real frames
  near the target timestamp before committing — a split-screen layout can put
  the actually-referenced UI element in a different region than the
  transcript alone would suggest.

Scene transitions:
- Wherever this episode's layout genuinely changes scene type (hero
  full-webcam <-> screen-recording+PIP), build a short (~0.4s) xfade+
  acrossfade crossfade between the two full segments rather than a hard cut
  — reuse build_transition()'s approach (real encoded duration via ffprobe
  for the offset, plain "fade" style, -pix_fmt yuv420p forced explicitly on
  the output to avoid a real pix_fmt-mismatch playback bug that shipped once
  this episode). Same-scene-type cuts don't need this.

Audio/captions:
- Caption chunking/timing per the established style (5-7 words, Geist Bold,
  darker/more opaque panel fill for legibility over varied backgrounds).
- Mic-indicator overlay ONLY on genuine live-dictation-to-Claude moments
  (sustained speech landing directly into a text input via voice-to-text) —
  verify against the actual transcript/footage, not just "there's a text box
  nearby." A wrong positive is worse than a missed one.
- Sound effects are NOT yet built for this series — if you add them, treat
  it as new work (pick a technique, verify it, document it in the style doc
  for next time), not something already established to reuse.

ONE CHECKPOINT: after building the EDL, give me a short plain-English
summary of the cut (shape, length, which beats got which treatment, what
graphics you're planning, which moments get shrink-aside vs. plain PIP) and
wait for a go-ahead before compositing. After that, build straight through
to a preview render without further check-ins.

STANDING PREFERENCES:
- Cost-conscious — batch similar sub-agent work, patch instead of rebuilding
  when possible, flag before anything that looks like a big token spend.
- Verify your own compositing work with fresh frame extraction (multiple
  points across a feature's full active window, not just the edges or the
  first frame) before telling me something's done. This exact pipeline has
  shipped "verified" sub-agent reports that were wrong multiple times this
  episode — a corner-PIP clipping bug, a card/webcam overlap reported as
  having "real margin" when it didn't, a grain-layer-scope claim. Don't
  relay a sub-agent's verification claim without an independent spot-check
  of your own, especially for overlay positioning, alpha compositing, or
  multi-state animations (hero/corner/mid-transition).
- If a style/technique choice changes or firms up this episode, update
  LIQUID_GLASS_STYLE.md and the template README before we're done, so the
  NEXT episode starts from the current state, not a stale one.

Go ahead and start with inventory + transcription.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Glob, Grep, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## 4bdddc46-3b80-45ec-bc37-523e74d4fda6
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL
- The user wants to build or extend a design system, design tokens, or component library
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

SKILLS (Prefer the skills shipped with the Figma plugin on the agent being used. If no Figma plugin is installed, use the skills served by the Figma MCP resource):
- /figma-use — MANDATORY before calling use_figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-use/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-design — for translating an app page or layout into Figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-library — for building a design system in Figma from code; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-library/SKILL.md
- /figma-code-connect — for mapping Figma components to codebase components; fallback: skill://figma/figma-code-connect/SKILL.md
- /figma-use-figjam — for FigJam-specific use_f

- hyperframes: Mandatory entry point: read this first for any request to make, create, edit, animate, or render a video, animation, or motion graphic, including a promo, explainer, captioned clip, title card, overlay, slideshow or interactive deck, Remotion port, or any HyperFrames HTML composition. Also use it to inspect, diagnose, validate, preview, publish, or batch-render an existing HyperFrames project. Inputs may be a website URL, GitHub PR, Figma design or URL, text or brief, existing footage, or music. It resumes project state, captures intent when applicable, selects and installs the owning workflow, and routes domain capabilities. HyperFrames is the default output framework unless the user explicitly chooses another framework for the deliverable or asks only to record a browser session.
- hyperframes-animation: All animation knowledge for HyperFrames — atomic motion rules, multi-phase scene blueprints, scene transitions, broader motion-design techniques, AND the seven runtime adapters (GSAP default, plus Lottie, Three.js, Anime.js, CSS keyframes, Web Animations API, TypeGPU). Use for any motion or animation task: pick 2-4 rules and compose, or load a blueprint, or look up runtime-specific API (e.g. GSAP eases / Lottie player / Three.js mixer). Also covers auditing an existing composition's choreography (animation map) and 24 named text-animation effects. HyperFrames-native: single paused timeline, seek-safe, deterministic.
- hyperframes-audio: Use when audio already placed in a HyperFrames composition needs to be mixed: fade-in/fade-out, crossfade, track gain or volume, volume automation, ducking, a music bed that fights a voiceover (voiceover carve), effects on a track (EQ, compressor, limiter, gate, saturation, delay, reverb, chorus, phaser, bitcrush), or automation envelopes drawn on a track's volume or any effect parameter. Don't use for sourcing or generating audio — finding BGM, SFX, or making a voiceover is `/media-use`. Don't use for clip timing or track layout, which is `/hyperframes-core`.
- hyperframes-cli: Use the HyperFrames CLI development loop: init, add, catalog, capture, lint, check, snapshot, compare, grade-compare, preview, play, present, beats, keyframes, single or batch render, publish, cloud, cloudrun, feedback, lambda, doctor, browser, info, upgrade, skills, compositions, docs, benchmark, telemetry, transcribe, auth, tts, and remove-background. Also use when diagnosing build or render failures. validate, inspect, and layout are deprecated aliases; use check. Covers local, HeyGen-hosted cloud, AWS Lambda, and Google Cloud Run rendering.
- hyperframes-core: The HyperFrames composition contract — build one renderable project. Use for composition structure, the `data-*` timing attributes, `class="clip"`, tracks, sub-compositions, variables, framework-owned media playback, deterministic-render rules, and validation. Also covers Tailwind projects and the STORYBOARD.md / SCRIPT.md plan formats. Read before writing composition HTML.
- hyperframes-creative: Non-animation creative direction for HyperFrames videos. Use for design spec (frame.md / design.md) handling, palettes, typography, narration, beat planning, audio-reactive visuals, composition patterns, and brand / style decisions. For atomic motion patterns and scene blueprints, use `hyperframes-animation`.
- hyperframes-keyframes: Use when a HyperFrames composition needs a punch-in, punch-out, zoom, reframe, Ken Burns treatment, camera move, visual match/whip handoff, or other seek-safe 2D/3D keyframes; also for GSAP, CSS keyframes, Anime.js, WAAPI, FLIP, paths, masks, SVG morph/draw, text trails, 3D depth, or `hyperframes keyframes` diagnostics. Don't use for broad scene strategy, brand design, media sourcing, captions, or general video planning.
- hyperframes-registry: Install, discover, and wire registry blocks and components into HyperFrames compositions. Use when running hyperframes add or hyperframes catalog, installing one item or every block matching a tag, wiring an installed item into index.html, or working with hyperframes.json. Covers discovery, install locations, block sub-composition wiring, component snippet merging, and authoring a new block or component to contribute upstream (idea → scaffold → validate → PR).
- media-use: Agent Media OS, the single skill for every media need in a HyperFrames project. Resolve BGM, SFX, image, icon, brand logo, voice, color grade, or LUT into a frozen local file or paste-ready block + ledger record (one verb, `resolve`); generate via TTS / music / image models when the catalog misses; produce voiceover, transcription, captions, and background removal through one shared audio engine; operate on media (cut / reframe / transform); and reuse assets across projects. Also use for vague feedback that real footage looks dark, flat, boring, should feel retro/camcorder/print/ASCII, needs privacy, or needs a media reveal.
- motion-graphics: A short, design-led motion graphic where motion is the message — kinetic typography, stat count-up, chart/data-viz hit, logo sting / brand lockup, lower-third / callout / social overlay, animated map (highlight regions, connect places, zoom to a location), animated tweet / news-article / headline, webpage / UI animation (scroll, cursor, callouts), or fusing a real image's geometry into a chart. Usually under 10s (up to ~30s), no narration or live-action subject; renders to MP4 or transparent overlay. Longer / narrated / multi-scene → /general-video. Unclear → /hyperframes.
- baz: Create professional motion graphics and videos from the terminal. AI-powered composition with multi-track layering, choreography, voiceovers, and Lambda rendering. Gated 5-phase workflow ensures quality.
- video-use: Edit any video by conversation. Transcribe, cut, color grade, generate overlay animations, burn subtitles — for talking heads, montages, tutorials, travel, interviews. No presets, no menus. Ask questions, confirm the plan, execute, iterate, persist. Production-correctness rules are hard; everything else is artistic freedom.
- figma:figma-code-connect: Creates and maintains Figma Code Connect template files that map Figma components to code snippets. Use when the user mentions Code Connect, Figma component mapping, design-to-code translation, or asks to create/update .figma.ts or .figma.js files.
- figma:figma-create-new-file: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE every `create_new_file` tool call. NEVER call `create_new_file` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user wants a new blank Figma file — a new design, FigJam, or Slides file — or when you need a fresh file before calling `use_figma`. Usage — /figma-create-new-file [editorType] [fileName] (e.g. /figma-create-new-file figjam My Whiteboard, /figma-create-new-file slides Q3 Review)
- figma:figma-design-to-code: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE calling the `get_design_context` Figma MCP tool. You MUST trigger this skill whenever the user wants to implement, build, port, or code up a Figma design as code. Example prompts (not exhaustive) are 'implement this Figma design', 'build this screen from Figma', 'turn this Figma into code', 'design to code'. This skill provides critical instructions and steps to the agent on how to correctly implement Figma designs in code and must NOT be skipped.
- figma:figma-generate-design: Use this skill alongside figma-use when the task involves translating an application page, view, or multi-section layout into Figma. Triggers: 'write to Figma', 'create in Figma from code', 'push page to Figma', 'take this app/page and build it in Figma', 'create a screen', 'build a landing page in Figma', 'update the Figma screen to match code', 'convert this modal/dialog/drawer/panel to Figma'. This is the preferred workflow skill whenever the user wants to build or update a full page, modal, dialog, drawer, sidebar, panel, or any composed multi-section view in Figma from code or a description. Discovers design system components, variables, and styles from Code Connect files, existing screens, and library search, then imports them and assembles views incrementally section-by-section using design system tokens instead of hardcoded values.
- figma:figma-generate-diagram: MANDATORY prerequisite — load this skill BEFORE every `generate_diagram` tool call. NEVER call `generate_diagram` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user asks to create, generate, draw, render, sketch, or build a diagram — flowchart, architecture diagram, sequence diagram, ERD or entity-relationship diagram, state diagram or state machine, gantt chart, or timeline. Also trigger when the user mentions Mermaid syntax or wants a system architecture, decision tree, dependency graph, API call flow, auth handshake, schema, or pipeline visualized in FigJam. Routes to type-specific guidance, sets universal Mermaid constraints, and tells you when to use a different diagram type or skip the tool entirely (mindmaps, pie charts, class diagrams, etc.).
- figma:figma-generate-library: Build or update a professional-grade design system in Figma from a codebase. Use when the user wants to create variables/tokens, build component libraries, create individual components with proper variant sets and variable bindings, set up theming (light/dark modes), document foundations, or reconcile gaps between code and Figma. Also use when the user asks to create or generate any component in Figma — even a single one — since components require proper variable foundations, variant states, and design token bindings to be production-quality. This skill teaches WHAT to build and in WHAT ORDER — it complements the `figma-use` skill which teaches HOW to call the Plugin API. Both skills should be loaded together.
- figma:figma-implement-motion: Translates Figma motion and animations into production-ready application code. Use when implementing animation/motion from a Figma design — user mentions "implement this motion", "add animation from Figma", "animate this component", provides a Figma URL whose node is animated, or when `get_design_context` returns motion data or instructs you to call `get_motion_context`.
- figma:figma-swiftui: SwiftUI ↔ Figma translation. Use whenever the user mentions Swift, SwiftUI, iOS, iPhone, or iPad — in EITHER direction — translating a Figma design into SwiftUI (design → code), or pushing SwiftUI views / screens / tokens back into a Figma file (code → design). Triggers on phrases like 'implement this Figma design in SwiftUI', 'build this screen in Swift', 'push this SwiftUI view to Figma', 'mirror my Swift code in a Figma file', or whenever a Figma URL appears alongside `.swift` files / an `.xcodeproj`. Routes to a direction-specific reference doc; loads alongside `figma-use` for the code → design path.
- figma:figma-use: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE every `use_figma` tool call. NEVER call `use_figma` directly without loading this skill first. Skipping it causes common, hard-to-debug failures. Trigger whenever the user wants to perform a write action or a unique read action that requires JavaScript execution in the Figma file context — e.g. create/edit/delete nodes, set up variables or tokens, build components and variants, modify auto-layout or fills, bind variables to properties, or inspect file structure programmatically.
- figma:figma-use-figjam: This skill helps agents use Figma's use_figma MCP tool in the FigJam context. Can be used alongside figma-use which has foundational context for using the use_figma tool.
- figma:figma-use-motion: Motion / animation context for the `use_figma` MCP tool — animating Figma nodes via manual keyframes, animation styles, easing, and timeline duration. Load alongside figma-use whenever a task involves adding, editing, or inspecting animation on a node.
- figma:figma-use-slides: This skill helps agents use Figma's use_figma MCP tool in the Slides context. Can be used alongside figma-use which has foundational context for using the use_figma tool.
- anthropic-skills:consolidate-memory: Reflective pass over your memory files — merge duplicates, fix stale facts, prune the index.
- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- anthropic-skills:explain-usage: Explain where this session's tokens went, with one simple chart in plain language. Use when the user says things like "explain my usage", "where did my tokens go", or asks for a usage breakdown.
- anthropic-skills:morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. # Vibe Coding Series — video template

Living reference for starting a new episode of "Vibe Coding till I reach one
paying customer" (Kodely). This is a pointer/checklist document, not a frozen
copy of assets — the canonical, most-current versions of everything it
references live in `first-video/edit/` and get pulled forward into each new
episode. Update this file (and `../../LIQUID_GLASS_STYLE.md`) whenever a
style/technique decision changes, so the next episode starts from the latest
state instead of re-deriving it.

## Style reference

Read `tools/video-use/LIQUID_GLASS_STYLE.md` first — full design-token and
technique reference (palette, glass-panel recipe, captions, neon border,
retrowave background, CRT transitions, scene-change crossfades, dynamic
webcam shrink-aside, mic indicator). Everything below points back into it.

## Starting a new episode

1. Copy the OBS Screen + Webcam recording pair into a new
   `<episode-name>/` folder under `Video Projects/` (not the OBS holding
   folders themselves).
2. Run the video-use skill's normal pipeline (transcribe → pack → strategy →
   EDL) as usual — this part is generic, not series-specific.
3. For the compositing script, start from
   `first-video/edit/scripts/composite_full.py` as the reference
   implementation rather than writing one from scratch. It already has
   working, verified implementations of:
   - the hero-stage full-webcam layout (`build_webcam_primary`) — retrowave
     background, resized/centered webcam, neon border, grain/flicker texture,
     optional background scrim
   - the screen-recording + webcam-PIP layout (`build_screen_primary`) —
     Ken-Burns zoom, position-slide, neon border tracking the PIP through
     slides
   - the dynamic shrink-aside behavior for when a motion-graphic card needs
     to appear during a hero-stage moment
   - scene-change crossfades between hero-stage and screen-recording beats
   - per-overlay CRT power-on/power-off transitions for motion-graphic cards
4. For the animated background/border assets, copy these slot directories
   from `first-video/edit/animations/` as a starting point (re-render only if
   a parameter genuinely needs to change for the new episode — loop speed,
   color, size — don't rebuild from scratch):
   - `slot_retrowave_bg_loop/` — animated synthwave background
   - `slot_neon_border_loop/` — animated neon webcam border
   - `slot_grain_flicker_loop/` — optional atmospheric grain/flicker overlay
5. For new one-off motion graphics (stat cards, title reveals, tag callouts),
   build fresh per-episode as usual — those are inherently tied to that
   episode's specific content, not reusable.
6. `helpers/crt_transition.py` is a drop-in reusable filter fragment — import
   it directly, no need to recreate the technique.

## Known-good parameter values (as of the first episode)

These are starting points, not permanent constants — confirm with Nick before
assuming they're still right for a new episode, especially loop speeds and
scrim opacity, which both took multiple rounds of "still too [fast/dark]"
feedback to land on.

- Retrowave background loop: ~20s per cycle, seeded star randomness
- Neon border: ~14.4s per comet lap, 576x432 r=28 box (or whatever the
  episode's webcam PIP size is), core thickness ~4.5px, base glow reach
  ~10-14px, comet glow reach ~24px, opacity: core ~0.55, glow layers
  ~0.1-0.3, comet layers stronger (~0.75-1.0 on the hot/white tiers)
- Background scrim: 25% opacity black, background plate only
- Hero webcam size: ~980px tall, source aspect preserved exactly
- Dynamic shrink-aside: 60-70% of hero size, ~0.5s eased transition each way
- Scene-change crossfade: 0.4s, plain `fade` style, `-pix_fmt yuv420p` forced
  explicitly on the output
- CRT transition: ~0.18s entrance/exit each

## Baz.studio comparison track (experimental, source-only)

`baz-assets/` holds Remotion/TSX scene sources built via the `baz` CLI, as a
side-by-side comparison against the HyperFrames assets above. Free to build
and iterate on (`baz scenes create`/`set-code`, no AI cost), but alpha-channel
export is currently broken on baz.studio's end (see that folder's README for
the exact repro and a bug-report ID) — so these aren't usable video assets
yet, just source + design reference. Check that README before investing more
time here; the export bug may be fixed by the time you read this.

## Hands-off starter prompt

Paste this at the start of a new episode's session to run mostly
autonomously (one checkpoint after the EDL, then straight through to a
preview render). It exists because a shorter "just reuse the reference
script" instruction leaves real gaps — a future session might not dig deep
enough into `composite_full.py` to notice everything that's in there. This
version spells out every established technique explicitly, including the
specific verification lesson from a bug that shipped this episode (a
motion-graphic card and the shrink-aside webcam box overlapped because only
the graphic's opening frame was checked, not its full active window).

Keep this prompt in sync with reality: if a technique below changes or a new
one gets established, update it here too, not just in the sections above.

```
New episode of my "Vibe Coding till I reach one paying customer" series.
Footage is in <folder>. Run this mostly autonomously — don't check in with me
at every step, use your judgment based on what's established below, and only
stop for things that are genuinely ambiguous or expensive to undo.

SETUP (read first, don't narrate this back to me):
- tools/video-use/templates/vibe-coding-series/README.md
- tools/video-use/LIQUID_GLASS_STYLE.md
- first-video/edit/scripts/composite_full.py as the reference implementation
  — read the actual functions (build_webcam_primary, build_screen_primary,
  overlay_chain, _hero_transform, main's transition-boundary logic), don't
  just skim the file. Every autonomous decision below has a working
  implementation somewhere in this file; find it and adapt it rather than
  reinventing the technique.
- Reuse first-video/edit/animations/slot_retrowave_bg_loop,
  slot_neon_border_loop, slot_grain_flicker_loop as-is unless this episode's
  content genuinely needs something different.

AUTONOMOUS DECISIONS (make the call yourself, don't ask):

Cut & pacing:
- Take selection, cut placement, pacing — use the established cut-craft
  rules (audio-first, preserve peaks, pad 30-200ms, snap to word boundaries).

Layout per beat:
- Full-webcam-hero vs. screen-recording+PIP for each beat — hero for pure
  talking-head/story sections, PIP for anything referencing what's on
  screen.
- PIP corner (bottom-left/bottom-right): check what's actually on screen at
  each placement, not just alternating corners arbitrarily — reposition
  away from anything the box would cover, with a smooth eased slide (never
  an instant teleport) when the corner changes mid-beat.
- The neon border must be present on the webcam at ALL times it's visible —
  hero mode, PIP mode, and through every PIP corner-to-corner slide — always
  tracking the webcam's exact current box/position, never static or
  disappearing during a transition.

Motion graphics:
- Which moments get a motion graphic — ground each one in a specific
  number/name/callout actually said, not generic decoration. Prefer a few
  well-placed graphics over covering every beat.
- Every motion-graphic card gets the CRT power-on/power-off transition
  (helpers/crt_transition.py) on entrance and exit — except a graphic that's
  a pure continuation across a hard footage cut (still mid-appearance, not a
  true first-appearance or final-disappearance), which should skip that
  edge rather than look like it's glitching/re-powering-on.
- Which graphic-carrying webcam-hero moments need the shrink-aside treatment
  (webcam scales to 60-70% of hero size and moves to whichever side is clear
  of the graphic, rather than cutting to tiny PIP mode). For each one: check
  the graphic's actual rendered content bounding box across its FULL
  duration, not just its opening frame — a placement that's clear at frame 1
  can still collide with the graphic later in its own animation. This
  exact mistake shipped once already this episode (a card and the aside
  webcam box overlapped because only the opening frame was checked) — verify
  with real frame extraction across the graphic's entire active window
  before considering a placement done, and require a genuine deliberate gap,
  not just "technically not touching by a couple pixels."
- Background scrim: a black overlay on the retrowave background PLATE ONLY
  (never the webcam/border/graphic content) — default 25% opacity, composited
  before the border/webcam are drawn on top. Skip the grain/flicker texture
  unless it's specifically wanted for this episode.

Zoom:
- Screen-recording beats only. Genuine focal points only — never decoration
  on broad layout commentary. Cap 2.0x. Verify targets against real frames
  near the target timestamp before committing — a split-screen layout can put
  the actually-referenced UI element in a different region than the
  transcript alone would suggest.

Scene transitions:
- Wherever this episode's layout genuinely changes scene type (hero
  full-webcam <-> screen-recording+PIP), build a short (~0.4s) xfade+
  acrossfade crossfade between the two full segments rather than a hard cut
  — reuse build_transition()'s approach (real encoded duration via ffprobe
  for the offset, plain "fade" style, -pix_fmt yuv420p forced explicitly on
  the output to avoid a real pix_fmt-mismatch playback bug that shipped once
  this episode). Same-scene-type cuts don't need this.

Audio/captions:
- Caption chunking/timing per the established style (5-7 words, Geist Bold,
  darker/more opaque panel fill for legibility over varied backgrounds).
- Mic-indicator overlay ONLY on genuine live-dictation-to-Claude moments
  (sustained speech landing directly into a text input via voice-to-text) —
  verify against the actual transcript/footage, not just "there's a text box
  nearby." A wrong positive is worse than a missed one.
- Sound effects are NOT yet built for this series — if you add them, treat
  it as new work (pick a technique, verify it, document it in the style doc
  for next time), not something already established to reuse.

ONE CHECKPOINT: after building the EDL, give me a short plain-English
summary of the cut (shape, length, which beats got which treatment, what
graphics you're planning, which moments get shrink-aside vs. plain PIP) and
wait for a go-ahead before compositing. After that, build straight through
to a preview render without further check-ins.

STANDING PREFERENCES:
- Cost-conscious — batch similar sub-agent work, patch instead of rebuilding
  when possible, flag before anything that looks like a big token spend.
- Verify your own compositing work with fresh frame extraction (multiple
  points across a feature's full active window, not just the edges or the
  first frame) before telling me something's done. This exact pipeline has
  shipped "verified" sub-agent reports that were wrong multiple times this
  episode — a corner-PIP clipping bug, a card/webcam overlap reported as
  having "real margin" when it didn't, a grain-layer-scope claim. Don't
  relay a sub-agent's verification claim without an independent spot-check
  of your own, especially for overlay positioning, alpha compositing, or
  multi-state animations (hero/corner/mid-transition).
- If a style/technique choice changes or firms up this episode, update
  LIQUID_GLASS_STYLE.md and the template README before we're done, so the
  NEXT episode starts from the current state, not a stale one.

Go ahead and start with inventory + transcription.
```

## Open items / still evolving

Keep this section updated — it's the fastest way for a future session to know
what's settled vs. still being iterated on.

- Neon border thickness/brightness went through several rounds this episode;
  confirm current values still read right before assuming final.
- Sound effects throughout — not yet implemented as of episode 1.
- Subtitles baked into the final render — cues generated, not yet confirmed
  baked into episode 1's final export.

- Neon border: ~14.4s per comet lap, 576x432 r=28 box (or whatever the
  episode's webcam PIP size is), core thickness ~4.5px, base glow reach
  ~10-14px, comet glow reach ~24px, opacity: core ~0.55, glow layers
  ~0.1-0.3, comet layers stronger (~0.75-1.0 on the hot/white tiers)
- Background scrim: 25% opacity black, background plate only
- Hero webcam size: ~980px tall, source aspect preserved exactly
- Dynamic shrink-aside: 60-70% of hero size, ~0.5s eased transition each way
- Scene-change crossfade: 0.4s, plain `fade` style, `-pix_fmt yuv420p` forced
  explicitly on the output
- CRT transition: ~0.18s entrance/exit each

## Baz.studio comparison track (experimental, source-only)

`baz-assets/` holds Remotion/TSX scene sources built via the `baz` CLI, as a
side-by-side comparison against the HyperFrames assets above. Free to build
and iterate on (`baz scenes create`/`set-code`, no AI cost), but alpha-channel
export is currently broken on baz.studio's end (see that folder's README for
the exact repro and a bug-report ID) — so these aren't usable video assets
yet, just source + design reference. Check that README before investing more
time here; the export bug may be fixed by the time you read this.

## Hands-off starter prompt

Paste this at the start of a new episode's session to run mostly
autonomously (one checkpoint after the EDL, then straight through to a
preview render). It exists because a shorter "just reuse the reference
script" instruction leaves real gaps — a future session might not dig deep
enough into `composite_full.py` to notice everything that's in there. This
version spells out every established technique explicitly, including the
specific verification lesson from a bug that shipped this episode (a
motion-graphic card and the shrink-aside webcam box overlapped because only
the graphic's opening frame was checked, not its full active window).

Keep this prompt in sync with reality: if a technique below changes or a new
one gets established, update it here too, not just in the sections above.

```
New episode of my "Vibe Coding till I reach one paying customer" series.
Footage is in <folder>. Run this mostly autonomously — don't check in with me
at every step, use your judgment based on what's established below, and only
stop for things that are genuinely ambiguous or expensive to undo.

SETUP (read first, don't narrate this back to me):
- tools/video-use/templates/vibe-coding-series/README.md
- tools/video-use/LIQUID_GLASS_STYLE.md
- first-video/edit/scripts/composite_full.py as the reference implementation
  — read the actual functions (build_webcam_primary, build_screen_primary,
  overlay_chain, _hero_transform, main's transition-boundary logic), don't
  just skim the file. Every autonomous decision below has a working
  implementation somewhere in this file; find it and adapt it rather than
  reinventing the technique.
- Reuse first-video/edit/animations/slot_retrowave_bg_loop,
  slot_neon_border_loop, slot_grain_flicker_loop as-is unless this episode's
  content genuinely needs something different.

AUTONOMOUS DECISIONS (make the call yourself, don't ask):

Cut & pacing:
- Take selection, cut placement, pacing — use the established cut-craft
  rules (audio-first, preserve peaks, pad 30-200ms, snap to word boundaries).

Layout per beat:
- Full-webcam-hero vs. screen-recording+PIP for each beat — hero for pure
  talking-head/story sections, PIP for anything referencing what's on
  screen.
- PIP corner (bottom-left/bottom-right): check what's actually on screen at
  each placement, not just alternating corners arbitrarily — reposition
  away from anything the box would cover, with a smooth eased slide (never
  an instant teleport) when the corner changes mid-beat.
- The neon border must be present on the webcam at ALL times it's visible —
  hero mode, PIP mode, and through every PIP corner-to-corner slide — always
  tracking the webcam's exact current box/position, never static or
  disappearing during a transition.

Motion graphics:
- Which moments get a motion graphic — ground each one in a specific
  number/name/callout actually said, not generic decoration. Prefer a few
  well-placed graphics over covering every beat.
- Every motion-graphic card gets the CRT power-on/power-off transition
  (helpers/crt_transition.py) on entrance and exit — except a graphic that's
  a pure continuation across a hard footage cut (still mid-appearance, not a
  true first-appearance or final-disappearance), which should skip that
  edge rather than look like it's glitching/re-powering-on.
- Which graphic-carrying webcam-hero moments need the shrink-aside treatment
  (webcam scales to 60-70% of hero size and moves to whichever side is clear
  of the graphic, rather than cutting to tiny PIP mode). For each one: check
  the graphic's actual rendered content bounding box across its FULL
  duration, not just its opening frame — a placement that's clear at frame 1
  can still collide with the graphic later in its own animation. This
  exact mistake shipped once already this episode (a card and the aside
  webcam box overlapped because only the opening frame was checked) — verify
  with real frame extraction across the graphic's entire active window
  before considering a placement done, and require a genuine deliberate gap,
  not just "technically not touching by a couple pixels."
- Background scrim: a black overlay on the retrowave background PLATE ONLY
  (never the webcam/border/graphic content) — default 25% opacity, composited
  before the border/webcam are drawn on top. Skip the grain/flicker texture
  unless it's specifically wanted for this episode.

Zoom:
- Screen-recording beats only. Genuine focal points only — never decoration
  on broad layout commentary. Cap 2.0x. Verify targets against real frames
  near the target timestamp before committing — a split-screen layout can put
  the actually-referenced UI element in a different region than the
  transcript alone would suggest.

Scene transitions:
- Wherever this episode's layout genuinely changes scene type (hero
  full-webcam <-> screen-recording+PIP), build a short (~0.4s) xfade+
  acrossfade crossfade between the two full segments rather than a hard cut
  — reuse build_transition()'s approach (real encoded duration via ffprobe
  for the offset, plain "fade" style, -pix_fmt yuv420p forced explicitly on
  the output to avoid a real pix_fmt-mismatch playback bug that shipped once
  this episode). Same-scene-type cuts don't need this.

Audio/captions:
- Caption chunking/timing per the established style (5-7 words, Geist Bold,
  darker/more opaque panel fill for legibility over varied backgrounds).
- Mic-indicator overlay ONLY on genuine live-dictation-to-Claude moments
  (sustained speech landing directly into a text input via voice-to-text) —
  verify against the actual transcript/footage, not just "there's a text box
  nearby." A wrong positive is worse than a missed one.
- Sound effects are NOT yet built for this series — if you add them, treat
  it as new work (pick a technique, verify it, document it in the style doc
  for next time), not something already established to reuse.

ONE CHECKPOINT: after building the EDL, give me a short plain-English
summary of the cut (shape, length, which beats got which treatment, what
graphics you're planning, which moments get shrink-aside vs. plain PIP) and
wait for a go-ahead before compositing. After that, build straight through
to a preview render without further check-ins.

STANDING PREFERENCES:
- Cost-conscious — batch similar sub-agent work, patch instead of rebuilding
  when possible, flag before anything that looks like a big token spend.
- Verify your own compositing work with fresh frame extraction (multiple
  points across a feature's full active window, not just the edges or the
  first frame) before telling me something's done. This exact pipeline has
  shipped "verified" sub-agent reports that were wrong multiple times this
  episode — a corner-PIP clipping bug, a card/webcam overlap reported as
  having "real margin" when it didn't, a grain-layer-scope claim. Don't
  relay a sub-agent's verification claim without an independent spot-check
  of your own, especially for overlay positioning, alpha compositing, or
  multi-state animations (hero/corner/mid-transition).
- If a style/technique choice changes or firms up this episode, update
  LIQUID_GLASS_STYLE.md and the template README before we're done, so the
  NEXT episode starts from the current state, not a stale one.

Go ahead and start with inventory + transcription.
```

# Liquid Glass style reference

Reusable design tokens for the "liquid glass" (iOS 26) motion-graphics style,
established across the Kodely / Vibe Coding series. Reuse these values for
new graphics unless the video calls for a different brand explicitly.

## Palette

Warm pink → peach → magenta gradient (Kodely's own brand gradient):

```css
--glass-accent-1: #ff7aa8; /* pink */
--glass-accent-2: #ffb37a; /* peach */
--glass-accent-3: #ff6fae; /* magenta-pink */
--glass-accent-4: #cf3fc4; /* magenta */
/* typical usage: linear-gradient(135deg, var(--glass-accent-1), var(--glass-accent-2), var(--glass-accent-4)) */
```

## Glass panel recipe

- Backdrop blur + saturation boost on whatever sits behind the panel (`backdrop-filter: blur(20px) saturate(1.4)`).
- Translucent fill, not solid: low-alpha white/brand-tinted background (~10-20% opacity), not a flat card color.
- Rounded corners, 20-32px radius depending on card size.
- Subtle white edge-highlight catching light at an angle (a `border` or inset gradient-masked ring, ~2-3px, ~40% opacity) -- this is the single most important cue that reads as "glass" rather than "flat card."
- Soft drop shadow, low opacity, generous blur -- glass should feel like it's floating, not pasted on.
- Optional: a one-shot diagonal sheen sweep on entrance (a light gradient streak animating across the panel) reads well for a reveal moment; skip it for anything that holds on screen a while, it gets busy.

## Motion

- Never linear easing. Ease-out cubic (`power2.out`/`power3.out`) for reveals landing on a payoff; ease-in cubic (`power2.in`) for exits.
- Never reveal two new elements simultaneously -- stagger, one beat at a time.
- Sync paydoffs to the actual spoken word/number, using real per-word timestamps from the transcript (`edit/transcripts/<source>.json`) -- never estimate timing from the phrase-level text alone.

## Captions

Glass-pill captions, bottom-center (clear of a corner webcam PIP), built via `helpers/gen_caption_cues.py` (chunk sizing) + a HyperFrames data-driven overlay (see `helpers/composite_pip.py`'s overlay pattern for how a long alpha-webm overlay gets composited).

- **Chunk size: 5-7 words per caption** (not 2-3 -- tried the tighter chunking first, client wanted longer lines). `--max-chunk 6` is a good default.
- **Font size: 36px** Geist Bold (800) -- tried 50px first, too large for 5-7 word lines; 36px reads clearly and wraps cleanly to 2 lines on the longest cues. Pill `max-width` ~1600px.
- **Panel fill must be more opaque than other liquid-glass elements** -- captions sit over constantly-changing (often bright/light) backgrounds, unlike a graphic authored against one known background. A near-invisible white wash that looks fine in isolation can vanish against a light page. Use a darker tinted fill (~rgba(20-36,10-15,18-30, 0.64-0.72)) with real backdrop-filter blur, not the lighter ~0.1-0.2 alpha used on other cards -- verify legibility by test-compositing over BOTH a solid white and a bright brand-color background, not just dark video content.
- Pop-in (not slow reveal) per cue: quick `back.out` scale+opacity, ~0.04-0.08s -- a slow multi-second entrance looks laggy against fast speech cadence.
- Skip captioning any EDL range whose layout already carries its own on-screen kinetic type (e.g. an intro graphic) -- `gen_caption_cues.py --skip-layout` handles this, default skips `intro_graphic`.

## Full-frame / long overlay lesson (learned the hard way)

Any overlay graphic composited near a webcam PIP must clear the corner it might land in -- and since a PIP can be positioned in EITHER bottom corner depending on the segment (see `composite_pip.py`'s `pip_position` field), a graphic can't assume only one corner is at risk. First version of a multi-step explainer graphic spanned nearly the full frame height and ended up drawn directly over the presenter's face. Fix: anchor content-heavy overlays to the TOP portion of the frame (roughly y: 60-520 out of 1080) and leave the entire bottom band (~y 520-1080) clear, rather than just avoiding one specific corner.

## Neon webcam border (FINALIZED -- animated loop, not a static PNG)

The static `make_pip_assets.py --neon-glow` PNG approach (see below) was superseded: the client wanted actual moving light ("lights moving around the box"), not a static rim. Final version is an animated HyperFrames loop (`slot_neon_border_loop`, SVG + GSAP), traced as a rounded-rect rail that sits **exactly** on the webcam's own box edge -- zero outward margin. Key lessons from three iteration rounds:

When a motion-graphic card needs to appear DURING a full-webcam "hero" moment, don't just draw the graphic on top of the webcam (covers the presenter) and don't shrink the webcam all the way down to the small screen-recording-PIP size either (reads as a jarring size mismatch and wastes the "hero" framing). Reusable design tokens for the "liquid glass" (iOS 26) motion-graphics style,

new graphics unless the video calls for a different brand explicitly.

## Palette

Warm pink → peach → magenta gradient (Kodely's own brand gradient):

```css
--glass-accent-1: #ff7aa8; /* pink */
--glass-accent-2: #ffb37a; /* peach */
--glass-accent-3: #ff6fae; /* magenta-pink */
--glass-accent-4: #cf3fc4; /* magenta */
/* typical usage: linear-gradient(135deg, var(--glass-accent-1), var(--glass-accent-2), var(--glass-accent-4)) */
```

## Glass panel recipe

- Backdrop blur + saturation boost on whatever sits behind the panel (`backdrop-filter: blur(20px) saturate(1.4)`).
- Translucent fill, not solid: low-alpha white/brand-tinted background (~10-20% opacity), not a flat card color.
- Rounded corners, 20-32px radius depending on card size.
- Subtle white edge-highlight catching light at an angle (a `border` or inset gradient-masked ring, ~2-3px, ~40% opacity) -- this is the single most important cue that reads as "glass" rather than "flat card."
- Soft drop shadow, low opacity, generous blur -- glass should feel like it's floating, not pasted on.
- Optional: a one-shot diagonal sheen sweep on entrance (a light gradient streak animating across the panel) reads well for a reveal moment; skip it for anything that holds on screen a while, it gets busy.

## Motion

- Never linear easing. Ease-out cubic (`power2.out`/`power3.out`) for reveals landing on a payoff; ease-in cubic (`power2.in`) for exits.
- Never reveal two new elements simultaneously -- stagger, one beat at a time.
- Sync paydoffs to the actual spoken word/number, using real per-word timestamps from the transcript (`edit/transcripts/<source>.json`) -- never estimate timing from the phrase-level text alone.

A small animated mic-icon-plus-audio-visualizer-waves overlay for moments where the presenter is genuinely dictating text into a chat input via voice-to-text (not just narrating over a UI). Only add this where it's a real live-dictation moment -- verify against the actual transcript/footage (a sustained stretch of speech landing directly into a text field, not just talking while a webpage happens to be on screen) rather than pattern-matching on "there's a text input box nearby." A wrong positive is worse than a missed one.

## Reusable code

- `helpers/make_pip_assets.py` -- generates the rounded-mask/shadow/ring PNGs for a webcam PIP in this style, plus an optional `--neon-glow` static rim-light asset (superseded by the animated neon border loop above, but still usable for a cheaper treatment).
- `helpers/composite_pip.py` -- composites webcam PIP / fullscreen / motion-graphic beats in this style; see its module docstring for the EDL schema.
- `helpers/zoom_filter.py` -- Ken-Burns push-in zoom, jitter-free (see its docstring for the ffmpeg gotchas it avoids -- worth reading before touching zoompan directly).
- `helpers/gen_caption_cues.py` -- output-timeline caption chunking from an EDL + transcript (see Captions section above for the chunk-size/font defaults established for this series).
- `helpers/crt_transition.py` -- the CRT power-on/power-off squash+flash transition filter fragment (see above).
- `first-video/edit/animations/slot_retrowave_bg_loop/` and `slot_neon_border_loop/` and `slot_grain_flicker_loop/` -- the finalized HyperFrames source for the retrowave background, neon border, and grain/flicker assets described above. When starting a new video in this series, copy these slot directories as a starting point rather than rebuilding from scratch, and only re-render if a parameter genuinely needs to change for the new video.
- `first-video/edit/scripts/composite_full.py` -- the reference implementation tying all of the above together (hero-stage layout, screen-recording+PIP layout, dynamic shrink-aside, scene-change crossfades, per-overlay CRT transitions). The most complete single example of how these pieces compose; read it before starting a new video's compositing script from scratch.

## Alpha-transparent overlay graphics (HyperFrames → WebM)

When a HyperFrames motion graphic is meant to overlay (not replace) existing
footage, render it to WebM with VP9 alpha and confirm transparency by actually
sampling pixel alpha values (corner should be `(0,0,0,0)`), not by trusting
`ffprobe`'s default `pix_fmt` report -- it can look opaque even when the file
carries real per-pixel alpha, because the report doesn't always reflect
`libvpx-vp9`'s alpha-aware decode path. When *compositing* such a file with
ffmpeg, always pass `-c:v libvpx-vp9` explicitly (confirmed necessary in this
environment: the native `vp9` decoder silently drops the alpha channel and
renders the graphic as an opaque box).

# Video Projects — editing studio setup

This folder is your raw-footage workspace. The editing tools live in `tools/` and are
wired up as Claude Code skills, so you edit by dropping footage in a folder and talking
to Claude Code — no manual timeline work.

## What's installed

- **[video-use](https://github.com/browser-use/video-use)** (`tools/video-use`, symlinked
  into `.claude/skills/video-use`) — transcribes footage, cuts filler words/dead silence
  on word boundaries, color grades, burns subtitles, and orchestrates motion-graphics
  overlays. This is the driver.
- **[hyperframes](https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes)** (`tools/hyperframes`,
  skills installed globally in `~/.claude/skills/hyperframes*`) — HTML-native motion
  graphics renderer. video-use calls out to it (or Remotion/Manim/PIL) to generate
  overlay animations, one per sub-agent, in parallel.
- **OBS Studio** (already installed, v30.1.2) — for recording yourself via webcam + mic.
  It already has a scene with a webcam source and `Mic/Aux` configured from prior use.
- Prerequisites: Node.js 24, ffmpeg 9.0, Python 3.12 + uv — all installed via winget,
  confirmed working via `npx hyperframes doctor`.

## Transcription: local by default, no API key

video-use's `helpers/transcribe.py` now defaults to **local transcription**
(`faster-whisper`, runs on-device, no signup, no cost) instead of the ElevenLabs Scribe
API it ships with upstream. Verified working end-to-end, including verbatim filler-word
capture ("um," "uh,").

- Trade-off: no speaker diarization (fine for solo talking-head recordings) and no
  audio-event tagging. If you ever record multi-speaker footage and want ElevenLabs'
  diarization, get a key at https://elevenlabs.io/app/settings/api-keys, put it in
  `tools/video-use/.env`, and ask for `--backend scribe` on that session.
- If cuts miss an audible "um"/"uh", ask for a bigger model
  (`--model medium` or `--model large-v3`, default is `small`) — bigger models capture
  disfluencies more verbatim, at the cost of transcription speed.
- Also fixed: the original helper scripts (`render.py`, `grade.py`, `pack_transcripts.py`,
  etc.) print arrows/±/≥ characters that crash on Windows' default console encoding —
  patched all of them to force UTF-8 output so a real render session won't die mid-run.

## Recording webcam + mic (OBS)

OBS Studio is already installed, with a webcam + `Mic/Aux` scene and two separate
recording outputs configured:

- `C:\Users\edmem\Videos\OBS\Webcam` — webcam+mic takes
- `C:\Users\edmem\Videos\OBS\Screen` — screen recordings

Workflow: **Start Recording** in OBS, do your take, **Stop Recording** — the file lands
in whichever of those two folders matches the active scene/output. Those folders are a
holding area, not a project workspace (OBS will keep dumping unrelated takes there over
time) — before editing, copy or move the specific take(s) you want into a subfolder here
under `Video Projects\`, e.g.:

```powershell
mkdir "Video Projects\launch-video"
move "C:\Users\edmem\Videos\OBS\Webcam\<your-take>.mkv" "Video Projects\launch-video\"
```

Then `cd` into that project subfolder and run `claude` — `edit/` gets created alongside

# Video Projects — editing studio setup

This folder is your raw-footage workspace. The editing tools live in `tools/` and are
wired up as Claude Code skills, so you edit by dropping footage in a folder and talking
to Claude Code — no manual timeline work.

## What's installed

- **[video-use](https://github.com/browser-use/video-use)** (`tools/video-use`, symlinked
  into `.claude/skills/video-use`) — transcribes footage, cuts filler words/dead silence
  on word boundaries, color grades, burns subtitles, and orchestrates motion-graphics
  overlays. This is the driver.
- **[hyperframes](https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes)** (`tools/hyperframes`,
  skills installed globally in `~/.claude/skills/hyperframes*`) — HTML-native motion
  graphics renderer. video-use calls out to it (or Remotion/Manim/PIL) to generate
  overlay animations, one per sub-agent, in parallel.
- **OBS Studio** (already installed, v30.1.2) — for recording yourself via webcam + mic.
  It already has a scene with a webcam source and `Mic/Aux` configured from prior use.
- Prerequisites: Node.js 24, ffmpeg 9.0, Python 3.12 + uv — all installed via winget,
  confirmed working via `npx hyperframes doctor`.

## Transcription: local by default, no API key

video-use's `helpers/transcribe.py` now defaults to **local transcription**
(`faster-whisper`, runs on-device, no signup, no cost) instead of the ElevenLabs Scribe
API it ships with upstream. Verified working end-to-end, including verbatim filler-word
capture ("um," "uh,").

- Trade-off: no speaker diarization (fine for solo talking-head recordings) and no
  audio-event tagging. If you ever record multi-speaker footage and want ElevenLabs'
  diarization, get a key at https://elevenlabs.io/app/settings/api-keys, put it in
  `tools/video-use/.env`, and ask for `--backend scribe` on that session.
- If cuts miss an audible "um"/"uh", ask for a bigger model
  (`--model medium` or `--model large-v3`, default is `small`) — bigger models capture
  disfluencies more verbatim, at the cost of transcription speed.
- Also fixed: the original helper scripts (`render.py`, `grade.py`, `pack_transcripts.py`,
  etc.) print arrows/±/≥ characters that crash on Windows' default console encoding —
  patched all of them to force UTF-8 output so a real render session won't die mid-run.

## Recording webcam + mic (OBS)

OBS Studio is already installed, with a webcam + `Mic/Aux` scene and two separate
recording outputs configured:

- `C:\Users\edmem\Videos\OBS\Webcam` — webcam+mic takes
- `C:\Users\edmem\Videos\OBS\Screen` — screen recordings

Workflow: **Start Recording** in OBS, do your take, **Stop Recording** — the file lands
in whichever of those two folders matches the active scene/output. Those folders are a
holding area, not a project workspace (OBS will keep dumping unrelated takes there over
time) — before editing, copy or move the specific take(s) you want into a subfolder here
under `Video Projects\`, e.g.:

```powershell
mkdir "Video Projects\launch-video"
move "C:\Users\edmem\Videos\OBS\Webcam\<your-take>.mkv" "Video Projects\launch-video\"
```

Then `cd` into that project subfolder and run `claude` — `edit/` gets created alongside
the footage there, per the daily workflow below.

"""Pack all Scribe transcripts in <edit>/transcripts/ into one readable markdown.

Groups word-level entries into phrase-level lines, breaking on any silence
>= 0.5s OR speaker change. Each phrase gets a [start-end] prefix. This is
the PRIMARY artifact the editor sub-agent reads to pick cuts — it fits one
hour of takes in a tenth the tokens of raw Scribe JSON and gives
word-boundary precision from text alone.

Output: <edit>/takes_packed.md

Usage:
    python helpers/pack_transcripts.py --edit-dir <edit_dir>
    python helpers/pack_transcripts.py --edit-dir <edit_dir> --silence-threshold 0.5
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import sys

# Windows consoles default to cp1252, which can't encode the arrows/±/≥ used
# in progress output below — force UTF-8 so this doesn't crash mid-run.
sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
sys.stderr.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
from pathlib import Path


def format_time(seconds: float) -> str:
    """Format a time in seconds as "NNN.NN" with fixed 6-char width for alignment."""
    return f"{seconds:06.2f}"


def format_duration(seconds: float) -> str:
    """Format a duration as "Ms" or "Mm SSs"."""
    if seconds < 60:
        return f"{seconds:.1f}s"
    m = int(seconds // 60)
    s = seconds - m * 60
    return f"{m}m {s:04.1f}s"


def group_into_phrases(
    words: list[dict],
    silence_threshold: float = 0.5,
) -> list[dict]:
    """Walk a Scribe word list, break into phrases on silence >= threshold
    OR speaker change. Returns list of {start, end, text, speaker_id}.

    Scribe `words` entries have types 'word', 'spacing', or 'audio_event'.
    We keep 'word' and 'audio_event' content in phrase text. 'spacing'
    entries carry the silence information via their start/end times.
    """
    phrases: list[dict] = []
    current_words: list[dict] = []
    current_start: float | None = None
    current_speaker: str | None = None

    def flush() -> None:
        nonlocal current_words, current_start, current_speaker

"""Full per-segment compositing pass: webcam PIP (rounded/shadow/ring) or
fullscreen blur-fill webcam, plus Ken-Burns zoompan pushes on specific
screen_primary segments, per-segment 30ms audio fades (screen audio only),
then concat. Mirrors render.py's Hard-Rule-2 shape (composite-then-concat)
but extended for dual-source (screen+webcam) compositing, which render.py
doesn't support natively.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import json
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")

HELPERS_DIR = Path(r"C:\Users\edmem\OneDrive\Desktop\Video Projects\tools\video-use\helpers")
sys.path.insert(0, str(HELPERS_DIR))
from crt_transition import crt_transition_filter  # noqa: E402

ROOT = Path(r"C:\Users\edmem\OneDrive\Desktop\Video Projects\first-video")
EDIT = ROOT / "edit"
SCREEN = str(ROOT / "screen.mp4")
WEBCAM = str(ROOT / "webcam.mp4")
ASSETS = EDIT / "assets"
CLIPS = EDIT / "clips_composited"
CLIPS.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

# --- "hero stage" webcam_primary background/treatment assets ---------------
RETROWAVE_BG = EDIT / "animations" / "slot_retrowave_bg_loop" / "render.mp4"  # 1920x1080 60fps 10.0s opaque, seamless loop
GRAIN_LOOP = EDIT / "animations" / "slot_grain_flicker_loop" / "render.webm"  # 1920x1080 60fps 2.5s VP9 alpha
NEON_BORDER = EDIT / "animations" / "slot_neon_border_loop" / "render.webm"  # 1920x1080 60fps 14.4s VP9 alpha (confirmed via ffprobe; redesigned since this comment was first written)

# Optional background darken (build_webcam_primary's apply_scrim=True), used
# for the demo_60s_v2 mockup. Still being iterated on -- adjust freely, this
# is the one knob to change.
SCRIM_OPACITY = 0.25

# webcam.mp4 is exactly 640x480 (4:3, confirmed via ffprobe) -- target height
# 980px preserves that aspect exactly via scale=-2:980 (ffmpeg's -2 rounds the
# computed width to the nearest even integer: 980*640/480 = 1306.67 -> 1306).
HERO_W, HERO_H = 1306, 980
HERO_X, HERO_Y = round((1920 - HERO_W) / 2), round((1080 - HERO_H) / 2)  # 307, 50

# The neon border loop was authored for a 576x432 PIP centered on the 1920x1080
# canvas (same center as the new hero webcam, since HERO_X+HERO_W/2 == 960 and
# HERO_Y+HERO_H/2 == 540 too). Scaling the whole border frame around its own
# center by HERO_H/PIP_H exactly grows the traced rail from the old 576x432
# box to the new HERO_W x HERO_H box (both ~4:3, so one scalar works for both
# axes -- verified: 576*S = 1306.67 matches HERO_W, matching the unrounded
# hero width to within rounding noise). See report for the frame-level check.
NEON_SCALE_HERO = 980 / 432  # ~2.268519
# Same derivation, for the ASIDE resting state: the border loop's native
# 576x432 authored footprint scaled to ASIDE_H's height (ASIDE_W/ASIDE_H is
# the same ~4:3 as the border's own aspect, same reasoning as NEON_SCALE_HERO
# above). Since ASIDE_H is itself just HERO_H*ASIDE_SCALE, this is exactly
# NEON_SCALE_HERO*ASIDE_SCALE -- the border scales down by the SAME factor
# the webcam itself scales down by, continuously, at every point in between
# (see _hero_transform / the dynamic branch of build_webcam_primary).
NEON_SCALE_ASIDE = 638 / 432  # ~1.476852

# Ranges where the webcam shrinks ASIDE (not down to the tiny PIP size) while
# its own graphic overlay is on screen (see OVERLAYS[5]/[18] windows below),
# then grows back. Redesigned per user feedback: previously this shrank all
# the way down to the standard 576x432 PIP size in a bottom corner (the same
# size used behind screen_primary segments) -- the user explicitly does not
# want that; they want a ~30-40% reduction from HERO size (i.e. resting at
# 60-70% of hero), moved to whichever side of the screen the graphic's real
# content doesn't occupy, so the two sit side by side instead of the graphic
# sprawling behind a tiny corner PIP.
DYNAMIC_SHRINK_RANGES = {5, 18}
SHRINK_DUR = 0.5  # seconds, eased shrink/slide aside and back (0.4-0.6s per spec)

# Content-bbox investigation (extracted+inspected frames spread across each
# graphic's FULL active window, not just its opening frame -- see report):
#   slot_bank_stat (range 5, 10.2s): glass card bottom-LEFT, card box
#     x~90-730,y~590-940, readable "$128 CAD" glyphs only occupy x~90-520 --
#     the whole right half of the frame (x>730) is clear for its entire
#     window.
#   slot_codely_reveal (range 18's 1st overlay, 3.2s): glass PILL/CARD BOX
#     (not just its text) bottom-CENTER, x~590-1330,y~680-950 -- confirmed
#     via index.html: the card is centered (left:50%,top:812px, translate
#     -50%/-50%) and NEVER moves horizontally or past its full scale=1 extent
#     (entrance/exit only scale the box DOWN from 1.0 and nudge y by
#     +/-10-22px, both of which shrink the box toward its center -- so
#     y~680-950 is the true worst-case/full extent of the card box for the
#     graphic's ENTIRE 3.2s window, not just one sampled frame). A prior
#     version of this fix rested the webcam box's bottom edge at y=719,
#     clearing only the "Codely" TEXT band (y~740-910) but NOT the actual
